title: ASU Hockey Coach Suspended; Hospitalized Player Faces Grim Prognosis, Family Attorney Claims
body:
ASU’s men’s hockey program was thrown into turmoil on Wednesday when the university placed head coach Greg Powers on administrative leave in the wake of a harrowing incident that left sophomore forward Matthew Mayich in critical condition. Mayich, 21, collapsed from severe heat‑related illness during a summer conditioning session on August 20, prompting an emergency response that has left the athlete fighting for his life and raised questions about the safety protocols for outdoor training in the desert climate.

The incident unfolded on a sweltering afternoon at the university’s practice field, where the team was conducting a routine cardio workout under direct sun. According to teammates, Mayich began to stumble and fell to the ground, displaying classic signs of heatstroke: rapid heartbeat, confusion, and an inability to speak. Athletic trainers and campus medical staff rushed him to a nearby hospital, where doctors confirmed he was suffering from extreme heatstroke, a condition that can cause irreversible organ damage if not treated within minutes. As of the latest update, Mayich remains on life support, and his family’s attorney has warned that his chances of recovery are “extremely slim.”

In response, Arizona State University announced that Powers would be placed on leave pending a comprehensive review of the circumstances surrounding the workout. The university’s statement emphasized a commitment to “thoroughly investigate all aspects of the training regimen, supervision, and environmental conditions that may have contributed to this tragic event.” While the university has not detailed the specific findings that triggered the leave, the decision aligns with a growing trend in collegiate athletics to hold coaching staff accountable for player safety, especially in high‑risk environments.

The episode has reignited a broader conversation about heat safety in college sports, a concern that has intensified over the past decade as climate change drives temperatures higher across the Southwest. The National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) issued updated heat‑illness guidelines in 2022, urging schools to adopt heat‑index monitoring, provide ample hydration breaks, and schedule outdoor activities during cooler hours. Critics argue that many programs, particularly those with limited resources, still fall short of these standards. In Arizona, where summer temperatures routinely exceed 100 °F (38 °C), the margin for error is razor‑thin, and the Mayich case may become a catalyst for stricter enforcement.

Former players and athletic staff have voiced mixed reactions. Some former teammates praised Powers for his long‑standing dedication to the program, noting that he has previously emphasized conditioning and player welfare. Others, however, questioned whether the intensity of the summer workout was appropriate given the extreme heat. “We’ve always trusted the coaching staff to keep us safe,” said a former ASU hockey player who asked to remain anonymous. “When the temperature spikes, you expect extra precautions, not a grueling cardio session under the blazing sun.”

Legal experts suggest that the university could face liability if investigations reveal negligence in planning or supervising the workout. The attorney representing Mayich’s family has indicated that a civil suit is likely, citing “failure to implement adequate heat‑stroke prevention measures” as a potential cause of action. In similar cases, universities have settled for substantial sums, prompting many institutions to reevaluate risk management strategies and invest in heat‑monitoring technology, such as wearable sensors that alert staff to early signs of overheating.

Looking ahead, ASU’s athletic department has pledged to conduct a full audit of its training protocols and to collaborate with medical professionals to redesign its conditioning programs. The university also announced plans to host a series of workshops for coaches across all sports, focusing on heat‑illness recognition and emergency response. While the immediate future of the hockey program remains uncertain, the incident serves as a stark reminder that athlete safety must evolve in step with environmental realities. As the Sun Devils community rallies around Mayich and his family, the hope is that this tragedy will spur lasting changes that protect student‑athletes from the unforgiving desert heat.
